title: Freight Scales Offer
subject: Contracts
stem: On May 3, after learning that Naomi was expanding her courier business, Timothy emailed Naomi offering to sell several used parcel scales. Naomi replied on May 10 that she would buy the scales for $725 if Timothy delivered them to her loading dock on July 2. On June 4, Naomi decided to rent scales instead and wrote Timothy a message saying that she was no longer interested. Before she sent it, Timothy arrived at her dispatch office. As Naomi opened the door, Timothy said, "I can bring those parcel scales tomorrow. I only need to borrow James's box truck." Naomi said, "No, I do not want them," and handed Timothy the unsent message.
call: How should Timothy's June 4 statement most likely be characterized?

choices.A: A ratification of Naomi's May 10 acceptance of Timothy's earlier offer.

rightExplanation: Timothy's statement is best characterized as an offer. Naomi's May 10 reply did not accept Timothy's earlier offer on its own terms. It proposed a purchase only if Timothy delivered the scales to her loading dock on a specified date. Because that proposal called for delivery as the operative acceptance, Timothy's June 4 promise to bring the scales later was not itself an acceptance. It did, however, show willingness to sell the scales on the stated price-and-delivery terms, so it could be treated as a new offer.

wrongExplanations.A: The ratification label is tempting because Naomi had answered Timothy's original email. Her reply changed the legal posture by making delivery the condition for being bound; there was no prior acceptance for Timothy to ratify.
wrongExplanations.B: Borrowing a truck sounds like logistics have started. But Timothy only said what he intended to do later; he had not begun the requested delivery performance.
wrongExplanations.D: The statement tracks Naomi's proposed deal closely. But where the proposed deal made delivery the act that would bind the parties, a promise to deliver later does not complete acceptance.
